title: Enterprise Voice AI: How to Evaluate Security, Vendors, and Scale
summary: Evaluate enterprise voice AI security by tracing call data, reviewing subprocessors, inspecting failed calls, and testing capacity before procurement.
body_markdown:
Before signing an enterprise voice AI agreement, ask for the data-flow diagram, supplier list, incident procedure, and capacity commitment. You will need all four to understand what you are buying.


Across the deployments we've reviewed, conversation work tends to finish before the operational dependencies do. One program waited on a telephony license. Another lost three weeks to a contact center migration. A third could not start because the agent lacked a single CRM permission. The demo couldn't solve any of those.


### **Map the data before the conversation**#


In healthcare, the infrastructure conversation often happens before anyone discusses what the agent will say. Audio, transcripts, recordings, tool requests, and logs all need a place on the data map, with the provider, region, access rules, and retention settings attached.


List every company in that path, including cloud and carrier, and what each can see. Bland's[published subprocessor list](https://www.bland.ai/legal/subprocessors) is the starting point for confirming which providers apply to the proposed configuration.


A telehealth provider was missing prescription renewals and sometimes billing before patients had been serviced. It put Bland at the front of calls to identify the request, route it, and collect renewals for the clinical team. Before taking a patient call, the agent passed the team's most severe prompt-injection test.


Have your legal and security teams review the contracts for each provider handling that data.[HHS guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html) explains that a cloud provider maintaining electronic protected health information can be a business associate even when it cannot decrypt it. Include the relevant agreements, backups, support access, and deletion rules in the review.


### **When a call fails, find out why**#


Suppose the agent tells a patient an appointment has moved, but the calendar still shows the original time. Have the team inspect the workflow version, timing, tool request, and response. A failed write and an agent claiming success too early need different fixes.


Bland's[Call Details API](https://docs.bland.ai/api-v1/get/calls-id) gives your team call metadata, transcripts, and transfer information. Establish which traces your team can pull directly, which need a support request, and who joins the investigation.


Model changes have their own release and rollback responsibilities, covered in[why Bland builds its own models](https://www.bland.ai/blog/why-bland-builds-own-voice-ai-models) ; the incident procedure should name the people who can act on each part of the service.


### **Capacity means your busiest few minutes**#


A storm concentrates claims calls into a few minutes. The capacity requirement includes how many calls arrive together, how quickly traffic grows, and how long conversations last. It also includes the carrier, account lookups, claims database, and people receiving transfers.


[Bland's enterprise pricing](https://www.bland.ai/pricing) sizes concurrency to customer volume. Put peak capacity, provisioning arrangements, and overflow behavior in the agreement, then test the complete path. More AI capacity doesn't make a slow claims database faster.


### **Work without an owner stays undone**#


In one deployment, carrier registration and spam-labeling work went unstarted for six to seven months after launch. Nobody had been assigned to it. By the team's own account, nobody from the calling world came in, and the work never made it into a job description.


Carrier registration, number reputation, routing, permissions, and incident response need named owners before launch. So does reviewing changes after launch. Assign each responsibility to someone with the time and authority to act.


Return to the four documents before signing. Each should describe this deployment and identify who keeps it current.
